flags: The standard interpretation is that n is a positive integer, so 2n denotes an even number of radii.

question: A circular disk is divided by \(2n\) equally spaced radii \((n\gt0)\) and one secant line. The maximum number of nonoverlapping areas into which the disk can be divided is:
solution:
Under the conventional interpretation, assume that \(n\) is a positive integer. Equal spacing then pairs each radius with an opposite radius, producing \(n\) diameters. This pairing helps bound how many times the secant can cross the existing divisions. Initially, the radii make \(2n\) sectors.

The part of the secant inside the disk is a chord. If it coincides with an existing diameter, it adds no regions. Otherwise, it meets each diameter at most once. Thus there are at most \(n\) distinct interior crossing points, dividing the chord into at most \(n+1\) pieces. Each piece can split one existing sector into two, adding at most one region. Therefore the total is at most
\[
2n+(n+1)=3n+1.
\]
A secant through the center and distinct from every existing diameter has just one distinct crossing point and adds two regions. When \(n=1\), this attains four regions; when \(n>1\), it gives fewer than the upper bound.

To attain the bound for every positive integer \(n\), start with a line through the center whose direction differs from every diameter, and slide it a sufficiently small nonzero distance without rotating it. Its intersections with all the diameters can be kept close to the center, so they all lie inside the disk. The \(n\) crossings are distinct because different diameters meet only at the center, which the shifted line avoids. Each sector has angle at most \(180^\circ\), so a straight chord cannot leave and then return to the same sector. Consequently, the \(n+1\) chord pieces split \(n+1\) different sectors, attaining \(3n+1\) regions.

There is a qualification in the displayed wording: only \(n>0\) is stated. If \(n=3/2\), there are three radii spaced \(120^\circ\) apart. A secant avoiding the center can cross at most two: the crossed radii must point into the same open half-plane bounded by the parallel line through the center, and that half-plane cannot contain all three directions. It therefore adds at most three regions. A secant through the center adds at most two. To attain six regions, join the endpoints of two radii and shift that line slightly toward the center, keeping it parallel. It crosses both radii internally and splits all three sectors, giving \(3+3=6\), rather than \(3n+1=11/2\).

Thus the maximum is \(\boxed{3n+1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\), under the positive-integer convention for \(n\); the displayed condition alone does not justify an unconditional choice.
